stem: The demand function for a commodity is D(p) = 400 - 5p, where p is the price. The price elasticity of demand is defined as E = (dD/dp) * (p / D). What is the price elasticity of demand when the price p = 40?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Reporting just dD/dp = -5 without multiplying by p/D, i.e., reading the elasticity as the slope of the demand curve alone.
Using p/D instead of (dD/dp)*(p/D): E = p/D = 40/200 = 1/5, omitting the derivative dD/dp entirely from the formula.
Using D/p instead of (dD/dp)*(p/D): E = D/p = 200/40 = 5, inverting both the formula direction and ignoring the derivative.

explanation: The price elasticity formula is E = (dD/dp)*(p/D). Compute each part: dD/dp = -5 (constant slope). At p=40: D = 400-5*40 = 200. So E = (-5)*(40/200) = (-5)*(1/5) = -1. An elasticity of -1 indicates unit elastic demand at this price.

explanation_sections.punchline: All three parts of the elasticity formula must be assembled: the derivative dD/dp, the current price p, and the current demand D; none can be dropped.
explanation_sections.approach: Elasticity formula application: (1) differentiate D(p) to get dD/dp, (2) evaluate D at the given p, (3) multiply: E = (dD/dp)*(p/D). Check units: E is dimensionless.
explanation_sections.lesson: Price elasticity is not just the demand slope (dD/dp) and not just the ratio (p/D); it is their product. Omitting either factor gives a wrong answer.
explanation_sections.timing: 60-80 seconds. The calculation is two multiplications once you have D(40)=200 and dD/dp=-5: -5 * 40/200 = -5 * 0.2 = -1.
